name: Commelina

project_scope.mode: Photo-led Hays/Central Texas identification; canonical species C. erecta
project_scope.admission: C. erecta already canonical with project native-range PASS; this lesson adds no new taxon or county claims.
project_scope.lookalikes: Tinantia anomala and Tradescantia spp. canonical in Commelinaceae; introduced Commelina communis included ONLY as a comparison (not installed).
project_scope.rights_note: 3 real, physically installed and public-safe Commelina erecta photographs in this genus gallery. Original Calvin observation all-rights-reserved private-study only; Nathan Taylor flower macro CC BY-NC study/noncommercial; neither silently relabeled as unrestricted public.

look_here_first: DON'T stop at two BLUE PETALS. Follow the flower stem DOWN to its enclosing BRACT: Commelina flowers emerge from a folded green SPATHE (a leaflike bract making a shelter for buds and young fruit). In C. erecta the spathe margins are joined/CONNATE along a long basal portion. By contrast, local Tinantia anomala has a mostly FLAT open subtending bract and an EXPOSED one-sided cyme. Then zoom in: Commelina has THREE fertile stamens plus THREE sterile STAMINODES; Tinantia has SIX fertile stamens with distinctive bearded filaments.

genus_diagnostics.habit: Annual or perennial soft-stemmed herbs, often branched, with conspicuously JOINTED stems; several species can root at lower nodes. Local C. erecta is usually a perennial, not the introduced annual C. communis.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: ALTERNATE leaves with mostly parallel veins; each blade emerges from a conspicuous basal SHEATH wrapping the jointed stem. A sheath is part of a regular leaf—different from the separate green SPATHE that encloses flowers.
genus_diagnostics.spathe: SPECIAL GENUS CLUE: the inflorescence is subtended by a folded, boatlike or funnel-like GREEN SPATHE containing one/two short flower branches (cincinni). Spathe margins vary within Commelina: LONG CONNATE in C. erecta, mostly FREE/OPEN in C. communis, so do not claim all species have a fused pocket.
genus_diagnostics.flower: Flowers BILATERAL (zygomorphic), usually two conspicuous larger upper/lateral blue petals and one much smaller pale third petal; three sepals also exist, though behind the petals. Flower color/size overlap with Tinantia; folded spathe distinguishes genus more readily.
genus_diagnostics.stamens: Typically THREE fertile stamens (bearing pollen-producing anthers) and THREE STAMINODES (sterile, showy yellow antherlike ANTHERODES); fertile filaments are usually GLABROUS or smooth. Tinantia has SIX fertile stamens, several with long conspicuous colorful filamental hairs.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Small flower clusters (cincinni/cymes) are held INSIDE the folded spathe; buds and developing capsules may be hidden. Tinantia's terminal one-sided cyme is plainly above an open leaflike bract.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: A 2–3-chambered CAPSULE, not a berry or legume; in C. erecta usually 3-locular and usually two-valved. Young fruit remains protected in the spathe. Capsule/seed anatomy needs a confirmed local macro.

shared_traits: A Commelinaceae stem is usually jointed with parallel-veined, sheathing leaves and short-lived 3-sepal/3-petal flowers.
Commelina inflorescences emerge from SPATHE bracts; the relative fusion of spathe margins differentiates C. erecta from some other Commelina species.
The distinctive reproductive plan is 3 fertile stamens plus 3 staminodes; photo certainty must be established for counts, not assumed from distant flowers.
priority: SEE: open blue flower and locate the tiny pale third petal.
SPOT: trace flower to the folded GREEN SPATHE, separate from ordinary leaf sheath.
NAME: spathe, connate margins, sheathing leaf, fertile stamen, sterile staminode/antherode, style.
COMPARE: Tinantia open one-sided cyme, Tradescantia three similar petals, introduced Commelina communis open spathe.
REMEMBER: Blue petals are not enough; a flower tucked in a folded spathe is a stronger dayflower clue.
cautions: Petal colors, blue/purple tones, and two large petals overlap Commelina and Tinantia.
Fused spathe margins distinguish C. erecta from C. communis but are NOT universal to genus Commelina.
The small green coverings on Tinantia buds are SEPALS; they are not an enclosed Commelina spathe.
C. erecta has geographically varied leaf widths/flower colors; use a combination of traits.

quick_key.if: Blue/lavender flower with 2 very large petals and tiny third petal
quick_key.then: Follow the flower down: is there a folded pocket enclosing buds? If yes, Commelina door; if not, inspect Tinantia exposed cyme.

quick_key.if: Broad GREEN folded spathe with margins joined for a long distance
quick_key.then: Commelina erecta candidate. Confirm sheathing leaves, 3 fertile stamens plus 3 yellow staminodes, and fruit in spathe.

quick_key.if: Open folded spathe with clearly separate/unfused margins; 2 large blue petals
quick_key.then: Compare introduced Commelina communis, not automatically C. erecta; check real seam and floral/anther traits.

quick_key.if: Open, FLAT leaflike bract under a terminal one-sided exposed cyme, no pocket
quick_key.then: Tinantia anomala (false dayflower): check 6 fertile stamens, showy violet and pale-yellow filament beards, strongly clasping upper leaves.

quick_key.if: Three more evenly showy petals, often six conspicuously hairy fertile filaments and paired terminal cymes
quick_key.then: Tradescantia spiderworts; inspect sepal/flower, hair on filaments and different bract architecture.
Identify family provisionally by parallel-veined sheathing leaves and jointed nodes; wait for spathe/flowers to separate genera.

comparison_cards.title: TRUE DAYFLOWER vs FALSE DAYFLOWER — Commelina erecta vs Tinantia anomala
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Forget blue flowers at first: inspect the STRUCTURE directly beneath buds. A Commelina erecta spathe is folded/connate into a pocket; Tinantia flowers are on an exposed one-sided cyme ABOVE a flat bract.

field_matrix.commelina: Folded green enclosing SPATHE; buds concealed
field_matrix.tinantia: Mostly FLAT/open subtending leaflike bract, cyme exposed
6 fertile stamens; 5 with obvious bearded hair tufts

field_matrix.commelina: Generally perennial, sometimes rooting near base; auriculate sheath
field_matrix.tinantia: Typically annual in Central Texas; broad upper leaves often clasp stem

field_matrix.commelina: Installed exact-species spathe and sheath views; restricted filament macro in species lesson
field_matrix.tinantia: Existing species has public external bract/flower images and private Joey/River macro studies; don't equate external with installed

comparison_cards.caution: A green boatlike sepal enclosing EACH Tinantia bud is not a genus-level Commelina spathe. Spathe shape and true filaments beat petal color.

comparison_cards.title: TRUE DAYFLOWER vs INTRODUCED ASIATIC DAYFLOWER — C. erecta vs C. communis
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both have nearly the same showy two-blue-petal flower and both have a green spathe. Carefully inspect SPATHE MARGINS: long-connate in erecta vs distinct/open in communis.

field_matrix.communis: Often annual rooting at lower nodes
3 fertile + 3 sterile; no easy split from count

field_matrix.erecta: Installed spathe side view (seam dissection still needed)
field_matrix.communis: Comparison species not currently canonical in learner

comparison_cards.caution: Do not claim every Commelina flower belongs to erecta. An OPEN spathe isn't enough alone to conclude communis without full key and regional source.

comparison_cards.title: DAYFLOWER vs SPIDERWORT — Commelina vs Tradescantia
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Commelina has two very large petals + tiny pale third, and flowers tucked into a folded spathe. Local spiderworts typically have three evenly sized showy petals with six fertile stamens.

field_matrix.tradescantia: 6 fertile with often visibly bearded filaments
Terminal clusters subtended by bracts but no dayflower pocket

comparison_cards.caution: Both have parallel-veined sheathing leaves, which indicate family but do not decide genus.

visual_comparison.title: Commelina dayflowers — look inside the green folded spathe
visual_comparison.subtitle: THREE public-safe physically installed C. erecta images (flower, sheath, folded spathe), followed by TWO explicitly EXTERNAL licensed Tinantia comparison photos. The genus-stamen details in Calvin/Nathan/Joey limited-use species photos are NOT redistributed here.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BLUE FLOWER → GREEN SPATHE → 3 FERTILE STAMENS + 3 STAMINODES. FALSE DAYFLOWER = exposed cyme + FLAT bract + 6 hairy fertile stamens.

part_examples.title: 1 · SEE the blue flower
part_examples.look_for: Two conspicuously large rounded BLUE petals stand above a much smaller pale third petal. The flower has THREE petals, not merely two; the little third one is easy to overlook in a front view. The three sepals are behind the corolla, not confidently visible here.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Introduces the asymmetrical (ZYGOMORPHIC) dayflower flower plan without miscounting petals.

part_examples.title: 2 · SPOT the leaf SHEATH at a node
part_examples.role: closed or encircling sheathing leaf base / node
part_examples.look_for: The green blade leaves the stem toward upper left while a pale, elongated SHEATH runs downward hugging the vertical stem. Tiny hair tufts are visible at the sheath's top edge. Do not confuse this leaf sheath with the flowering spathe.
part_examples.why_it_matters: This is a strong Commelinaceae clue even when the blue flowers have shut for the day.

part_examples.title: 3 · NAME the folded SPATHE
part_examples.look_for: Find the broad, folded GREEN pocket directly below the emerging flower. This bract is the SPATHE. In C. erecta its margins are joined for a substantial length (CONNATE), but the actual joined seam still needs its own opened, labeled macro.
part_examples.why_it_matters: More useful than petal color for separating erected dayflower from open-bracted Tinantia and from an open-spathed Commelina communis.

part_examples.title: 4 · COMPARE bracts, not blue petals
part_examples.role: Commelina closed spathe vs Tinantia open subtending bract
part_examples.look_for: The illustrated flower buds emerge FROM a folded pocket. For false dayflower Tinantia, follow flowers down to an EXPOSED ONE-SIDED CYME above a mostly FLAT leaflike bract; small green sepals around each Tinantia bud are NOT a Commelina spathe.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Both plants have two large blue/lavender petals, so their inflorescence architecture is a better tie-breaker.

part_examples.title: 5 · NEED PUBLIC PHOTO — count fertile stamens
part_examples.look_for: An existing exact C. erecta flower macro shows 3 fertile stamens and 3 yellow cross-shaped ANTHERODES (sterile staminodes) with generally smooth filaments, but it is CC BY-NC and private-study only. Find an independently rights-cleared, close face-on flower showing the stamens, STAMINODES and STYLE with original pixel verification.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Commelina's 3 fertile + 3 sterile stamens are crucial against Tinantia's six fertile stamens and bearded filaments.

part_examples.title: 6 · NEED PHOTO — open the fused spathe seam
part_examples.role: spathe dissection showing connate basal margins
part_examples.look_for: Dissect ONE species-verified C. erecta spathe and photograph both sides with mm ruler, showing which green margins are actually FUSED and the internal buds. Compare at matched scale with Commelina communis's OPEN spathe and Tinantia anomala's flat bract.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The installed green-spathe photo shows the outer folded shape but cannot prove seam fusion itself.

part_examples.title: 7 · NEED PHOTO — fruit hidden inside the spathe
part_examples.look_for: Photograph an opened mature spathe and a split brown capsule showing the 3-locular ovary pattern, capsule valves and seeds. Match a flower view to a fruit view on the same plant when feasible.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Connects dayflower floral parts to the fruit and avoids confusing the green spathe with a pod.

part_examples.title: 8 · NEED LICENSED MATCH — Tinantia stamens and exposed cyme
part_examples.role: false dayflower / upper leaves clasp stem / filament beards
part_examples.look_for: Side-by-side genuine Tinantia anomala exposed cyme (not folded) and a close view of the 6 fertile stamens: five of six filaments bear conspicuous purplish/yellow beadlike hairs. Existing close-ups in species learner are CC BY-NC/other limited permissions; verify reuse on every intended image.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Explains why false dayflower belongs to the same family, but has a different reproductive architecture.

visual_comparison.annotation_policy: All three examples were inspected at image level. The outer spathe shape and sheath hairs are visually confirmed; joined spathe seam, seed locules, and stigma/staminode count are NOT shown with approved arrow coordinates.
